frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains a major market for Algerian gas, creating leverage but also exposure to shifting demand, pricing pressure, and competing Mediterranean suppliers.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya complicates border security and transit infrastructure while increasing pressure for external security cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: External Oil and Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain central to state financing, while foreign operators, lenders, and commodity-price volatility constrain policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Influence
frictionVectors.details: U.S., European, and Chinese competition around the Lobito Corridor is expanding infrastructure options but risks turning transport and mineral access into geopolitical leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Border and Transit Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger have disrupted established trade routes and exposed Benin's dependence on regional political stability and port access.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign-backed port, road, and logistics projects support growth but create long-term exposure to external creditors and strategic operators.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Partnership Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for greater value capture and domestic beneficiation as diamond-market weakness tests the long-standing state-private partnership.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Processing Capacity
frictionVectors.details: New critical-mineral opportunities could reduce diamond dependence, but limited local processing and infrastructure leave the country reliant on foreign capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Sovereignty Drive
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking tighter state control over gold production and foreign mining interests, but informal extraction, smuggling, and limited regulatory capacity weaken implementation.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Expanded reliance on Russian-linked security support reduces Western influence but creates new external dependence while insecurity continues to threaten mines, roads, and agricultural zones.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Governance
frictionVectors.details: Gold and rare-mineral activity remains vulnerable to informal networks, opaque licensing, and foreign-linked trading channels. Limited state capacity constrains Burundi's ability to capture full value from its resources.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over armed groups and cross-border accusations. Persistent insecurity raises transport costs and complicates regional infrastructure and trade integration.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and Praia offer growing maritime, logistics, and security value to external partners, including European, American, and Chinese actors. Competition creates investment opportunities but can narrow Cabo Verde's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: External Economic Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, remittances, and imported energy dominate the economic model, leaving the country exposed to external shocks. Water scarcity and high energy costs further limit domestic control over essential infrastructure.

highlights: Oil and Gas Under External Dependence

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon and Mining Capture
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, and emerging mining projects remain dependent on foreign capital, contractors, and trading networks. Revenue transparency and local value addition remain insufficient for strong sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Territorial Conflict
frictionVectors.details: The Anglophone conflict threatens roads, pipelines, and commercial activity in the southwest and northwest. Chinese-backed infrastructure and regional transport corridors expand connectivity but also increase financial and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Diamond Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Armed actors, foreign security partners, and informal traders compete for control of gold and diamonds. Weak regulation and insecurity prevent the state from reliably converting resource activity into public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bangui relies heavily on Russian-linked security support while maintaining ties with regional and international institutions. This dependence strengthens regime survival but can reduce transparency over mining access and strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Oil Revenue Still Defines State Power

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Oil Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal sovereignty remains tied to oil production and export infrastructure managed through external commercial partnerships. Price volatility, opaque revenue management, and limited domestic refining constrain broader economic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Balancing
frictionVectors.details: The government is recalibrating long-standing French security ties while managing pressure from Sudan's war and instability across the Sahel. External military and financial relationships remain central to regime security and border control.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains administrative control of Mayotte, making sovereignty a persistent diplomatic grievance and limiting Comoros' control over surrounding maritime resources. The dispute also shapes migration and security cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, imported energy, and foreign-funded infrastructure. Limited state capacity constrains its ability to independently develop fisheries, ports, and offshore economic resources.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to undermine Kinshasa's territorial control and threatens mining zones, transport corridors, and civilian access to resources. Rwanda-related tensions remain central to the security crisis.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Contract Imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt remain strategically valuable but are shaped by foreign capital, opaque intermediaries, and weak enforcement capacity. Kinshasa is seeking greater value capture while balancing Chinese commercial dominance with growing Western critical-minerals engagement.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues remain central to state finances and expose Brazzaville to price volatility and external commercial influence. Limited diversification leaves local communities with modest gains from resource extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and resource-linked financing have expanded infrastructure but increased dependence on external contractors and creditors. Port, road, and energy projects remain vulnerable to opaque terms and weak oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Cocoa Processing
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening local processing and producer regulation, but multinational firms still dominate financing, trading, and premium-market access. Low farm incomes and land pressures continue to limit sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas and Strategic Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil and gas development is improving energy prospects while increasing reliance on international operators and technology providers. Abidjan must balance investment attraction with revenue transparency and domestic industrial participation.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Presence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities, but this creates strategic dependence and exposes the country to great-power rivalry. Port and security decisions are closely tied to external patrons.

frictionVectors.title: Doraleh and Ethiopia Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's economy depends heavily on port access for Ethiopia and on externally financed logistics infrastructure. Debt exposure and competition with alternative regional corridors constrain the state's bargaining power over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and asset dependence
frictionVectors.details: External financing from Gulf states and international lenders is strengthening Egypt's liquidity but increasing foreign influence over strategic land, ports, and infrastructure assets.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, leaving Egypt exposed to perceived risks to downstream water security and regional bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling hydrocarbon output is increasing pressure on Equatorial Guinea's fiscal model and its reliance on foreign operators, technical expertise, and new gas investments.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Major construction and energy projects remain vulnerable to opaque contracting, creditor leverage, and external commercial interests despite strong formal state ownership.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concentration
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains exposed to a small number of foreign-linked mining operations, limiting Eritrea's ability to retain value and diversify resource control.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Strategic competition around the Red Sea increases the value of Eritrean ports and coastline while raising risks of foreign basing pressure and regional entanglement.

frictionVectors.title: Customs and market dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's access to regional trade, customs revenue, energy, and transport networks remains heavily tied to South Africa, limiting independent economic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and forestry exposure
frictionVectors.details: Export agriculture and forestry depend on external markets and foreign-linked value chains, leaving domestic resource capture vulnerable to price shifts and corporate bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Nile negotiations
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's control over GERD is a major sovereignty gain, but unresolved arrangements with Egypt and Sudan continue to generate diplomatic and security friction.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and dependence on external finance constrain Addis Ababa's room to maneuver over telecoms, logistics, energy, and other strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Transition seeks tighter state control over oil and mining
Libreville rebalances legacy French economic ties

frictionVectors.title: Oil and manganese contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are pressing for greater domestic participation and fiscal returns from hydrocarbon and manganese projects. Renegotiation risks disputes with established foreign operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and port operations remain reliant on foreign capital and expertise. Efforts to diversify partners may create short-term financing and execution gaps.

highlights: Senegal-linked trade and security ties deepen

frictionVectors.title: Senegambia security and border dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional security cooperation and transport connectivity. This supports stability but limits independent strategic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Port and coastal resource vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Banjul port modernization and fisheries management attract foreign commercial interests. Weak enforcement raises concerns over revenue leakage and unauthorized fishing.

highlights: Gold and emerging lithium sectors face governance pressure

frictionVectors.title: Mining value-chain contest
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms remain central to gold production, while lithium development is prompting debate over local processing and state participation. Illegal mining continues to damage land, water, and public authority.

frictionVectors.title: IMF-linked fiscal constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and external financing conditions narrow Accra's policy space. Fiscal reforms can stabilize the economy but may limit state spending on strategic infrastructure and industrial development.

highlights: Junta accelerates bauxite and Simandou development
Resource nationalism rises faster than institutional accountability

frictionVectors.title: Simandou strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore and rail corridor is drawing major foreign investment and could transform export capacity. Guinea's leverage is substantial, but dependence on external operators, finance, and infrastructure remains high.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite expansion and local grievances
frictionVectors.details: Rapid bauxite growth generates state revenue while intensifying land, water, and displacement disputes. The military-led government faces pressure to demonstrate that resource nationalism benefits communities rather than only central authorities.

highlights: Cashew economy remains vulnerable to external price and buyer power
Political fragility weakens control of ports and coastal waters

frictionVectors.title: Cashew export dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy relies heavily on raw cashew exports, leaving producers exposed to foreign traders, volatile prices, and limited domestic processing. This constrains value capture and fiscal resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime and narcotics security
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and limited coastal enforcement create openings for illicit trafficking and external criminal networks. Dependence on international security assistance underscores the state's limited control over maritime sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure continues to constrain Nairobi's bargaining power with China, Gulf investors, and multilateral lenders over ports, rail, and energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Governance
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in Kenya's mineral and renewable-energy sectors is growing, while local-content rules and licensing capacity remain uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's fiscal and infrastructure position remains closely tied to water transfers to South Africa, limiting autonomy in negotiating project terms and revenue allocation.

frictionVectors.title: Remittance and Labor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on South African employment, logistics, and markets exposes Lesotho to policy shifts beyond its direct control.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Gold Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-controlled mining projects remain central to growth, but revenue capture, environmental safeguards, and community benefits are persistent sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and related logistics infrastructure attract competing external interests, creating leverage over trade corridors and national revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Blockades
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to treat oil production and export infrastructure as bargaining tools, weakening unified state control.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign military, political, and commercial actors retain influence through rival Libyan institutions, complicating efforts to secure sovereign control over infrastructure and borders.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed mining operations provide investment and exports but leave Madagascar exposed to external pricing, financing, and ownership decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Renewable Infrastructure Gap
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on external capital for electricity and transport infrastructure can restrict policy space while limiting domestic value capture from strategic resources.

highlights: Fertilizer and fuel dependence strains sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: INPUT AND FOREIGN-EXCHANGE VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Malawi remains heavily exposed to imported fuel, fertilizer, and food inputs, while chronic foreign-exchange shortages limit policy autonomy. IMF-backed reforms are stabilizing the macroeconomic framework but constrain near-term spending flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: MINING GOVERNANCE PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: New uranium and rare-earth prospects are attracting foreign capital, creating opportunities for revenue diversification. Weak institutional capacity and contract-transparency concerns could leave the state with limited value capture.

highlights: Russian security partnership replaces Western ties

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SECTOR SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are asserting greater control over industrial mining and state participation, especially in gold. This may increase public capture, but opaque renegotiations and insecurity risk deterring investment and reducing production.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIA-BACKED SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Security cooperation with Russia and the Africa Corps has displaced French and broader Western involvement. The arrangement expands regime autonomy rhetorically while creating dependence on an external military and political patron.

highlights: Iron and fisheries remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: GREATER TORTUE AHMEYIM DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Offshore gas production with Senegal is strengthening Mauritania's fiscal and diplomatic position, but the project relies on foreign operators, export infrastructure, and stable bilateral coordination. Delays or disputes could limit expected sovereign gains.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND FISHERIES VALUE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign participation remains central to iron-ore logistics and fisheries, while Chinese and Gulf-linked interests compete for access. Mauritania is seeking more domestic processing and tighter licensing, but enforcement capacity remains uneven.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS AND DIEGO GARCIA
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains intertwined with the future of the Diego Garcia military facility and wider Indian Ocean power competition. Any settlement must balance decolonization objectives with security ties involving the United States and United Kingdom.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND MARITIME COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is expanding its role in Indian Ocean shipping, logistics, and undersea-connectivity networks. Competing Indian, Chinese, Gulf, and Western commercial interests create opportunities but also pressure Port Louis to preserve strategic nonalignment.

highlights: Western Sahara remains core sovereignty front

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses control and development of Western Sahara to reinforce territorial claims, while phosphate, fisheries, and renewable-energy projects attract external partners. Legal challenges and disputes over local consent continue to complicate market access.

frictionVectors.title: EUROPEAN AND GULF CAPITAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: European investment, Gulf financing, and foreign technology support Morocco's renewables, ports, automotive, and hydrogen ambitions. These ties strengthen industrial capacity but expose strategic infrastructure and export plans to external bargaining power.

highlights: Cabo Delgado insurgency strains state reach

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to constrain government authority and delay major LNG projects. Mozambique remains reliant on foreign security assistance and multinational operators to protect strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Benefit Sharing
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led gas development could transform state revenues, but local employment, compensation, and revenue distribution remain politically sensitive.

highlights: Oil and green hydrogen raise strategic leverage

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries have attracted major foreign investors, creating pressure to secure strong local-content, taxation, and environmental terms before production begins.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European and other external capital is central to hydrogen development. Land, water use, export infrastructure, and domestic value capture remain potential sources of friction.

highlights: Junta asserts control over strategic minerals

frictionVectors.title: Oil Export Corridor
frictionVectors.details: The Niger-Benin oil pipeline remains vulnerable to diplomatic and security disruption, limiting the junta's ability to convert crude production into reliable state revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Realignment
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is renegotiating uranium and other mining relationships while reducing Western influence and expanding ties with Russia and regional partners, raising operational and sanctions risks.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Sabotage and Theft
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, vandalism, and insecurity continue to reduce export volumes and public revenue, weakening federal control over producing regions and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reforms and domestic refining improve leverage, but upstream investment, technology, and financing remain significantly dependent on international oil companies and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Networks
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security role and mineral-trade links in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo remain central sources of diplomatic pressure and allegations of indirect resource capture.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Strategic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Strong state capacity coexists with reliance on external aid, investment, and mineral markets, leaving Kigali exposed to donor scrutiny and supply-chain traceability demands.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA MARITIME CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Sao Tome and Principe depends on external partners to patrol its waters and protect fisheries and prospective offshore blocks. Maritime coordination with Nigeria remains central to managing overlapping security and resource interests.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign-funded infrastructure provides important connectivity but increases reliance on external capital. The government has limited fiscal space to negotiate from strength.

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND GAS CONTRACTS
frictionVectors.details: The Faye administration is pressing for greater state participation and contract review as Sangomar oil and GTA gas production develops. Tensions with international operators and lenders could rise if renegotiation is seen as destabilizing existing agreements.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND COASTAL INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Industrial foreign fishing and expanding energy infrastructure are straining coastal livelihoods. Senegal is seeking stronger local value capture while remaining dependent on external finance, technology, and export markets.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN FISHING ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles retains substantial regulatory control over its exclusive economic zone, but tuna access agreements and distant-water fleets create recurring sovereignty and sustainability concerns. Economic dependence on fisheries limits the government's room for abrupt restrictions.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: India, China, the United States, and European partners all seek maritime-security access and influence. Victoria is balancing these relationships to avoid strategic overdependence while protecting port and surveillance autonomy.

highlights: Local Control Struggles Against Foreign Capital

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND RUTILE GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed mining operations remain central to exports and public revenue, but contract disputes, environmental concerns, and demands for greater domestic processing continue. The state has leverage through licensing but remains dependent on outside capital and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: CHINA-LINKED INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders are important to transport and urban infrastructure development. Debt, procurement transparency, and repayment risks constrain Freetown's ability to convert infrastructure investment into durable sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: ETHIOPIA-SOMALILAND MARITIME DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Somalia rejects any external arrangement granting Ethiopia access through Somaliland without Mogadishu's consent. The dispute internationalizes control of ports, coastline, and potential offshore resources while complicating federal sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE HYDROCARBONS AND SECURITY PARTNERSHIPS
frictionVectors.details: Turkey and other external actors are becoming central to Somalia's maritime security and prospective energy development. Weak federal cohesion and al-Shabaab's continuing threat make resource licensing vulnerable to political fragmentation and unequal foreign influence.

highlights: Power and freight bottlenecks constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals influence
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is balancing Chinese, Western, and domestic interests in platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth supply chains. Pressure is growing to secure local processing rather than remain primarily an exporter.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and logistics strain
frictionVectors.details: Grid instability and weakened rail and port capacity limit industrial sovereignty and export reliability. Public-private reform is advancing, but infrastructure recovery remains vulnerable to fiscal and governance constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Oil transit vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on Sudanese export infrastructure, leaving its main revenue stream exposed to conflict, pipeline disruption, and bargaining pressure from Khartoum and external operators.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and external security leverage
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and armed mobilization constrain national control over oil-producing areas and transport corridors. Regional mediation and neighboring-state security interests continue to shape the peace process.

highlights: Red Sea access becomes strategic prize

frictionVectors.title: Externalized civil war
frictionVectors.details: Competing foreign support networks and arms flows are deepening the conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces. Gold, agricultural land, and trade routes remain central to wartime financing.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and inland transport corridors has become critical for humanitarian access, exports, and military logistics. Red Sea actors are seeking influence while state capacity remains severely weakened.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and LNG bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking to convert major offshore gas reserves into domestic industrial capacity and export revenue. Negotiations with international developers create tension over fiscal terms, local content, and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Transport-corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and logistics projects are attracting Gulf, Chinese, and Western interest as Tanzania strengthens its role as a gateway to landlocked neighbors. Diversification improves leverage but increases exposure to foreign financing and operating concessions.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hub

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is strategically important for Togo and neighboring Sahel markets, but its expansion depends on foreign capital, shipping networks, and regional political stability. Competition with other Gulf of Guinea ports limits bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability from the central Sahel are increasing pressure on northern Togo and its transport routes. Expanded security cooperation may improve resilience while also increasing reliance on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: European support for migration management and budget stability gives Brussels significant political leverage. Tunisia is resisting deeper conditionality while remaining dependent on external financing.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: High dependence on imported hydrocarbons and electricity exposes Tunisia to price shocks and supplier influence. Renewable projects are advancing but have not yet materially reduced this vulnerability.

highlights: Oil development tied to regional corridors

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sovereignty dispute
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to planned export revenues but faces financing, environmental, and human-rights pressure from Western actors. Kampala views the project as a test of its control over national resources.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail ambitions, and energy projects have expanded infrastructure capacity while increasing repayment and contract exposure. Uganda is seeking diversified partners without surrendering strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt investment from Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked firms is strengthening production prospects but intensifying competition over concessions, processing, and tax terms. Lusaka is pushing for more domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked policy constraints
frictionVectors.details: The IMF program and sovereign debt restructuring have improved macroeconomic credibility while narrowing fiscal room. External creditors retain influence over reform sequencing and infrastructure spending.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain prominent in lithium and other mineral projects, while Western and regional investors seek greater access. Export restrictions signal Harare's intent to force domestic processing, but enforcement and investment risks remain substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financial isolation
frictionVectors.details: Targeted sanctions, restricted market access, and weak correspondent banking channels limit Zimbabwe's ability to finance infrastructure and stabilize its currency. The government is compensating through mineral diplomacy and non-Western partnerships.
